entry.title: Peng Zhihui (ZhiHuiJun): The "Wild Iron Man" Who Built Robots in His Bedroom and Then Built a Company
entry.summary: Peng Zhihui, known across Chinese digital platforms by his online handle ZhiHuiJun, which translates roughly as "The Young Hui Gentleman," is one of the most unusual figures in Bilibili's history. He is simultaneously a creator with over 2.8 million followers, a former member of Huawei's…
entry.content:
Peng Zhihui, known across Chinese digital platforms by his online handle ZhiHuiJun, which translates roughly as "The Young Hui Gentleman," is one of the most unusual figures in Bilibili's history. He is simultaneously a creator with over 2.8 million followers, a former member of Huawei's elite "Genius Youth" program, and the co-founder, president, and chief technology officer of AgiBot, a robotics company valued in the billions. His story is not merely one of online fame but of a career trajectory that moved from bedroom tinkering to industrial-scale innovation without ever losing the creative curiosity that first attracted an audience. Born in 1993 in Ji'an, Jiangxi Province, Peng graduated from the University of Electronic Science and Technology of China (UESTC) with a bachelor's degree from the School of Life Science and Technology in 2015 and a master's degree from the School of Information and Communication Engineering in 2018.He then worked as an algorithm engineer at OPPO's AI Lab before joining Huawei's "Genius Youth" program in 2020, where he worked on Ascend AI chips and AI algorithms.In 2023, he left Huawei and co-founded AgiBot with his UESTC alumnus Deng Taihua, serving as the company's president and CTO.Throughout this entire period, he continued to upload videos to Bilibili under the name ZhiHuiJun, documenting his personal engineering projects with a level of technical depth and production quality that has made him a singular figure in China's maker community.

What sets ZhiHuiJun apart from virtually every other technology creator on Bilibili is the sheer ambition of the projects he undertakes as a solo creator. He does not review products or explain concepts from a distance; he builds things that most people would assume require a team of engineers and a well-funded laboratory. His breakout project, released in October 2021, was a small, high-precision six-axis robotic arm that he designed, built, programmed, and filmed entirely on his own. The arm, which he named Dummy, was capable of performing tasks as delicate as threading a needle through a grape's skin, and the video documenting its construction and operation accumulated millions of views and became one of the most discussed technology videos of the year in China.The project demonstrated not only his technical range, spanning mechanical design, industrial modeling, motor selection, control programming, and AI vision, but also his ability to communicate that complexity in a way that was engaging rather than intimidating. He followed Dummy with a series of equally ambitious projects: an autonomous bicycle that could balance itself and navigate without a rider, a miniaturized Linux computer the size of a coin, a modular mechanical keyboard, and a Mars rover constructed from crab shells.Each project was documented in a video that combined technical explanation, behind-the-scenes documentation of failures and iterations, and a narrative arc that made the final result feel earned rather than inevitable.

The stylistic signature of ZhiHuiJun's content is a combination of understated delivery and extraordinary technical substance. He does not rely on exaggerated reactions or dramatic editing; his voice is calm and matter-of-fact, and his videos often run fifteen to thirty minutes, a length that requires genuine viewer investment. What makes them compelling is the visible evidence of problem-solving. He shows the moments when a design fails, when a component does not work as expected, when he has to rethink an approach. This willingness to document the messy reality of engineering, rather than presenting only the polished final product, distinguishes him from creators who treat technology as a spectacle to be consumed rather than a practice to be understood. His audience, which includes both professional engineers and curious laypeople, responds to this authenticity. The nickname "Wild Iron Man" that fans gave him captures both the ambition of his projects and the do-it-yourself ethos that defines his creative identity.

ZhiHuiJun's platform achievements are substantial, though his follower count is smaller than that of some of Bilibili's most popular entertainment creators. As of January 2026, his Bilibili account has approximately 2.84 million followers, and his Weibo account has over one million.He was named a Bilibili Top 100 UP Creator for 2021, and his videos routinely accumulate millions of views. His influence, however, is not measured solely by platform metrics. In 2024, he was named to the Hurun China U30 list of young entrepreneurs and to Fortune China's 40 Under 40 list of business elites.In 2025, he was selected as one of the year's AI Figures, sharing the stage with Wang Xingxing, the founder of Unitree Robotics, a recognition that placed him among the most significant figures in China's embodied AI sector.His company, AgiBot, has become one of the leading players in China's humanoid robotics industry, and its 2025 acquisition of a controlling stake in the publicly listed Shangwei New Materials, valued at approximately 550 billion yuan, made him the chairman of a major A-share listed company at the age of thirty-two.

The broader significance of ZhiHuiJun's career lies in his demonstration that individual technical creativity and large-scale industrial ambition are not mutually exclusive. He began as a self-taught maker who used the Bilibili platform to share projects that no one had asked him to build, and he has ended up leading a company that is competing at the frontier of global robotics. His videos are not promotional content for his company; they are the record of a personal practice that predates and transcends his commercial success. For aspiring engineers and makers, he offers a model of how to develop deep technical skills through self-directed projects, how to communicate those skills to a broad audience without simplifying them into triviality, and how to transition from individual creativity to organizational leadership without abandoning the curiosity that started it all. His advice to students at his alma mater in 2026, that "good questions are becoming more precious than answers" and that "knowledge only becomes judgment after it is tested by practice," encapsulates a philosophy that is visible in everything he has built.

In summary, Peng Zhihui represents a distinctive model of the creator as engineer-entrepreneur, someone who built an audience by doing genuinely difficult things in public and then built an institution to do them at scale. His Bilibili channel is not merely a portfolio but a living archive of intellectual and practical development, from a coin-sized computer to a robotic arm capable of surgery-adjacent precision to the founding of a company that is now valued in the tens of billions. For Bilibili, he is evidence that the platform's technology section can nurture creators whose work has consequences far beyond the screen. For the broader landscape of Chinese innovation, he is a reminder that the most transformative careers often begin not with a business plan but with a camera, a workbench, and a stubborn refusal to accept that something is impossible.

entry.title: Zhiliaojieya Mengwu: The One-Man Studio Bringing the World's Most Overlooked Animals to Millions
entry.summary: Zhiliaojieya Mengwu, whose real name is Peng Xianbo, is a Chinese wildlife content creator and one of the most distinctive voices in Bilibili's knowledge section. Operating as a completely independent one-man studio, he has built an audience of over 4.3 million followers on Bilibili as…
entry.content:
Zhiliaojieya Mengwu, whose real name is Peng Xianbo, is a Chinese wildlife content creator and one of the most distinctive voices in Bilibili's knowledge section. Operating as a completely independent one-man studio, he has built an audience of over 4.3 million followers on Bilibili as of January 2025, with his content focused on the natural stories of rare, unconventional, and frequently misunderstood animals. His channel name, which translates roughly to "Got It, Stress-Relief Cute Creatures," is deliberately playful, but the work itself is anything but frivolous. Peng has been selected for Bilibili's annual Top 100 UP Creators list for three consecutive years, from 2022 through 2024, and in 2025 he received the platform's "Annual Public Welfare UP Creator" award, a recognition that reflects the social mission embedded in his work. His videos have been described as a "stress-relief zone for graduate school entrance exam preparation" and "the Animal World for a new generation," a formulation that captures both their calming effect and their role as an accessible entry point into natural history.

Peng Xianbo's path to becoming one of Bilibili's most recognized wildlife communicators was neither planned nor straightforward. During the COVID-19 pandemic, he found himself with time on his hands and turned to video creation as a way to make a living. His initial forays into the platform were in the guichu or "ghost畜" genre, a style of remix video that was popular on Bilibili at the time but which had begun to decline in both viewership and monetization potential. Recognizing that the format was no longer sustainable, he made a strategic pivot based on his academic background: he had studied animal medicine in university, and he decided to apply that training to a new creative direction. The transition was not immediate or easy. In the early period, his monthly income was only one or two thousand yuan, insufficient to cover his basic expenses, and each video required five to six days of production, with scripts exceeding two thousand words and AI voiceover meticulously adjusted for quality. He has since described those first two years as a period of "stubbornly grinding it out," during which he could barely afford rent and had to rely on sheer persistence to continue.

What distinguishes Zhiliaojieya Mengwu from the vast field of animal content on Chinese video platforms is his deliberate focus on species that most creators overlook. Rather than featuring domestic pets or the charismatic megafauna that dominate traditional wildlife programming, he specializes in snakes, insects, and other creatures that are typically regarded with fear, disgust, or indifference. His videos present these animals through a documentary-style approach, combining carefully sourced footage with humorous and accessible narration that reframes them as fascinating rather than threatening. He describes his own work as "non-serious science communication," a phrase that signals both his rejection of academic solemnity and his commitment to accuracy. His content operates on two distinct tracks: one track uses curated internet footage to create light, entertaining science videos that introduce viewers to animal behaviors and biological facts, while the other track involves original field documentation, often produced in collaboration with conservation organizations such as the SEE Foundation, to record wildlife in China's nature reserves and national parks. The latter track has taken him to locations such as the Chongzuo Nature Reserve in Guangxi, where he documented the white-headed langur and other protected species as part of a public welfare initiative with the mobile game Azur Lane. The structural variety of his output allows him to serve audiences with different levels of engagement, from casual viewers seeking entertainment to those genuinely interested in conservation and biodiversity.

Among his most representative works are videos such as "The Jaguar: What Era Are We Living In," "Failure Means Becoming a Box: The Courtship Stories of Unpopular Animals," and "Animal World's Version of Three Heroes Fighting Lu Bu: A Pride of Lions Takes On a Nile Crocodile". These titles exemplify his distinctive approach to naming and framing: they draw on internet slang, classical literary references, and absurdist humor to make the subject matter immediately engaging, while the content itself remains grounded in accurate biological information. His video about the Tibetan fox, titled "As Long As the Green Hills Remain," uses the animal's distinctive facial expression, which has become a meme in Chinese internet culture, as a hook to discuss its habitat, behavior, and conservation status. Another characteristic work, "The Clouded Leopard: Living Fossils of the Forest," combines footage of the rarely seen predator with narration that explains its evolutionary history and the threats it faces. His field documentation in Guangxi, produced with the SEE Foundation and featuring voice actor Ge Ping as an "animal observer," represents his most ambitious production to date, blending original footage with conservation messaging and a narrative structure that positions viewers as witnesses to the work of protecting endangered species.

The platform achievements of Zhiliaojieya Mengwu are substantial and reflect the growing appetite for science content on Bilibili. In June 2022, his rare animal science videos reached the top of Bilibili's "dark horse" growth chart, with his account gaining 1.148 million followers in a single quarter and a single-day peak of 57,700 new followers. At that time, his total follower count was only around 200,000, meaning that his growth during that period represented a more than fivefold increase. By January 2025, his follower count had reached 4.331 million, and his content has continued to accumulate millions of views across his video library. His three consecutive years on the Top 100 UP Creators list, from 2022 through 2024, place him among a select group of knowledge creators who have achieved sustained recognition, and his 2025 "Annual Public Welfare UP Creator" award specifically acknowledged the conservation dimension of his work. His selection alongside creators such as Luo Xiang, Lao Fanqie, Muyu Shuixin, and MediaStorm on the 2024 Top 100 list underscores his position within the platform's most influential cohort.

The broader social value of Peng Xianbo's work lies in his demonstration that conservation communication can be genuinely popular without resorting to either alarmism or sentimentality. By focusing on species that are typically ignored or feared, he expands his audience's understanding of biodiversity beyond the narrow range of animals that receive mainstream attention. His collaboration with conservation organizations and his participation in public welfare initiatives, including the "E Qi Shou Hu Di Qiu" environmental short video program organized by the SEE Foundation, position him as a bridge between digital content creation and on-the-ground conservation efforts. For viewers who may never encounter these animals in person, his videos offer a form of vicarious natural history education that is both entertaining and ethically grounded. His insistence on operating as a one-man studio, handling scripting, production, and business negotiations himself, also represents a distinctive model of independent creative practice that stands apart from the team-based structures of many comparable channels.

In summary, Zhiliaojieya Mengwu is a creator whose significance lies in his ability to find wonder in the overlooked corners of the natural world. He has built a successful career not by chasing trends or adopting the formats of his competitors, but by applying his academic training and personal curiosity to subjects that others have neglected. His three consecutive years on Bilibili's Top 100 list, his 4.3 million followers, and his 2025 public welfare award are all evidence that this approach has resonated with a large and loyal audience. For Bilibili, he represents the knowledge section at its most accessible and its most purposeful. For viewers, he offers a reminder that the most rewarding discoveries are often found in places we have been taught not to look. And for the broader landscape of Chinese digital culture, his career is a testament to the possibility of building a sustainable creative practice on the foundations of patience, expertise, and a genuine commitment to sharing the world's strangest and most wonderful creatures with anyone willing to pay attention.

entry.title: Muyu Shuixin: The Filmmaker Who Turned Long-Form Film Analysis into a National Classroom
entry.summary: Muyu Shuixin is a Chinese film and television commentator who has quietly become one of the most influential creators in Bilibili's history. Unlike many of his peers, he has never relied on viral gimmicks, shocking challenges, or personality-driven spectacle. Instead, he has built a career…
entry.content:
Muyu Shuixin is a Chinese film and television commentator who has quietly become one of the most influential creators in Bilibili's history. Unlike many of his peers, he has never relied on viral gimmicks, shocking challenges, or personality-driven spectacle. Instead, he has built a career on the patient, rigorous, and deeply literary analysis of films, television series, and animated works. His channel, which he began in August 2013 with an animation tutorial titled "Muyu Animation Classroom Episode 1: Insert Shots (FLCL)," has evolved over more than a decade into a cornerstone of Bilibili's film and television section, accumulating over 14 million followers and a reputation for intellectual seriousness that few creators on the platform can match. As of early 2025, his Bilibili account reported 14.05 million followers, and by late 2026 that number had grown to approximately 14.6 million, placing him among the platform's most-followed individual creators. His selection to Bilibili's Top 100 UP Creators list for eight consecutive years, from 2018 through 2025, is a distinction shared by only a handful of figures, and it reflects a sustained commitment to quality that has outlasted multiple cycles of platform trends.

Muyu Shuixin's personal background is deliberately obscure. He has never publicly disclosed his real name, his educational history, or the details of his early life, and he maintained a strict policy of not appearing on camera for the first decade of his career. When he finally revealed his face in a March 2024 video titled "After 10 Years as a Creator, an Introvert Finally Decides to Appear," he wore a mask, preserving the anonymity that had become a defining feature of his public persona. His channel name is derived from a classical Chinese idiom, "climbing a tree to seek fish and using clear water to mirror the heart" (缘木求鱼，白水鉴心), a phrase that suggests both the futility of certain pursuits and the value of self-reflection. This refusal to trade on personal biography is not merely a quirk; it is a deliberate artistic choice that directs the viewer's attention entirely to the work itself, to the films being analyzed and the ideas being explored. In an era when creator personality is often the primary product, Muyu Shuixin has built his audience on the strength of his analysis alone.

What distinguishes Muyu Shuixin's content from the vast field of Chinese film commentary is its extraordinary depth and its literary quality. His videos typically run between thirty and sixty minutes, and many of his most ambitious projects exceed that range significantly. His commentary is characterized by what Chinese media scholars have described as a multi-layered interpretive framework that includes close textual reading, artistic analysis, theoretical self-awareness, and real-world engagement. He does not merely summarize plots or offer superficial opinions; he situates each work within its historical context, compares different adaptations and source materials, and draws connections to broader cultural and philosophical questions. His voice, which has been described as magnetic and reminiscent of a late-night radio host, is a central element of his appeal, but it is the substance of his scripts that has earned him the loyalty of an audience that is willing to invest hours in a single video. He has been likened to a "video version of Dangnian Mingyue," a reference to the popular historian whose accessible yet rigorous writing brought the Ming dynasty to millions of readers, and the comparison captures the way his work functions as public education rather than mere entertainment.

His most celebrated achievement is arguably his fifty-episode, forty-five-minute-per-episode complete analysis of *Water Margin* (水浒传), one of China's four great classical novels. The series, which he began in late 2021, was not a simple retelling of the story but a comprehensive examination that incorporated multiple television adaptations, the original novel, related classical texts such as *The Thirty-Six Heroes of Song Jiang* and *The宣和遗事*, and folk theatrical traditions. Fans have compared his narration to the legendary storytelling of Shan Tianfang, a master of Chinese oral performance, and the series has been described as a "treasure of the platform" for its exhaustive research and clear presentation. Other major projects include his full analysis of *Dream of the Red Chamber*, his series on *The Romance of the Three Kingdoms*, his deep dive into *Records of the Grand Historian* (*Shiji*), and his interpretations of contemporary works such as *The Awakening Age* and *The Bad Kids*. His analysis of *The Bad Kids*, a drama about the moral complexity of juvenile crime, drew thousands of comments from viewers engaging with questions of narrative logic, cinematography, and social responsibility.

The commercial realities of Muyu Shuixin's career reveal the paradoxes of Bilibili's creator economy. In April 2023, he published a public statement acknowledging that he had not received a single advertising commission in over four months and that Bilibili's creator incentive payments were insufficient to cover his office rent. The disclosure, which came amid a broader debate about a "wave of creators stopping updates" on the platform, attracted widespread media attention and prompted reflection on the sustainability of long-form, high-cost content production. He described his work as "creating for love," a phrase that captured both his commitment to quality and his frustration with an economic model that struggled to support it. In 2024, he launched a paid membership program called "Starry Sky Reading Club," in which he appeared on camera for the first time (still wearing a mask), and he continued to update his *Shiji* series, demonstrating that his audience was willing to support his work directly. His ability to survive a period of financial precarity without compromising his creative standards is a testament to the loyalty he has cultivated and the perceived value of his output.

The social and cultural significance of Muyu Shuixin's work extends beyond the platform metrics. He has been credited with helping to legitimize long-form video analysis as a serious intellectual genre in China, demonstrating that viewers will commit hours of attention to content that treats them as capable of engaging with complex ideas. His videos on classical literature have functioned as a form of adult education, introducing millions of viewers to texts they might never have approached in written form. His decision to analyze *Water Margin* with reference to multiple adaptations and historical sources has been praised for encouraging viewers to think critically about the relationship between source material and adaptation, between historical context and contemporary interpretation. At a time when Chinese digital culture is often criticized for prioritizing speed and sensation over depth, Muyu Shuixin represents a counterexample: a creator who has built a massive audience by doing the opposite of what the algorithms supposedly reward.

In summary, Muyu Shuixin is a creator whose significance lies not in his personality but in his practice. He has demonstrated that anonymity, patience, and intellectual rigor can be viable foundations for a career in digital media, and that an audience exists for content that respects their time and their intelligence. His eight consecutive years on Bilibili's Top 100 list, his fourteen million followers, and his enduring influence on the platform's film and television section are all evidence of this. For Bilibili, he is a symbol of what the platform aspires to be when it takes its knowledge mission seriously. For viewers, he is a teacher in the truest sense, someone who does not merely explain what a film means but teaches how to watch, how to read, and how to think. And for the broader landscape of Chinese online culture, his career is a reminder that the most durable creative work is often the least performative, built not on the cult of personality but on the quiet accumulation of insight and craft.

entry.title: Xiao Yuehan Kehan: The Historian Who Built a Universe Out of Tongliao and Taught Millions to See the World from Below
entry.summary: Xiao Yuehan Kehan, whose real name is simply Xiao Yuehan, is a Chinese history content creator and one of the most influential figures in Bilibili's knowledge section. He is a native of Tongliao, a city in Inner Mongolia, and he operates his channel as a…
entry.content:
Xiao Yuehan Kehan, whose real name is simply Xiao Yuehan, is a Chinese history content creator and one of the most influential figures in Bilibili's knowledge section. He is a native of Tongliao, a city in Inner Mongolia, and he operates his channel as a solo creator, a fact that is all the more remarkable given the scale of his reach. As of March 2026, his Bilibili channel has over 10.62 million followers, making him the first creator in Bilibili's knowledge category to surpass the ten-million mark. Before becoming a video creator, he was an active answerer on Zhihu, the Chinese question-and-answer platform, where he wrote extensively on Soviet history, military affairs, and international politics under the name "Little John," a reference to the operational codename of Frank Underwood in the American television series *House of Cards*. His Zhihu answers accumulated a substantial following, and when he began uploading videos to Bilibili in November 2020, his early content consisted largely of curated selections from those written answers. His breakthrough was immediate: his first major video, "Why Was the Soviet Union So Powerful?", released on November 14, 2020, has accumulated over 33.9 million views as of August 2025, a figure that remains one of the highest in Bilibili's knowledge category.

What distinguishes Xiao Yuehan Kehan from the crowded field of Chinese history educators is his construction of an entire narrative and linguistic universe around a set of recurring themes and a highly distinctive lexicon. He organizes his content into several ongoing series. The "Bizarre Small Nations" series examines the histories of countries that are largely absent from mainstream historical discourse: The Gambia, Nauru, Burkina Faso, Albania, and dozens of others, each treated with the same seriousness and narrative care that larger nations typically receive. The "Hardcore Ruthless People" series abandons the traditional focus on kings, generals, and statesmen, instead telling the stories of criminals, con artists, spies, soldiers, and ordinary people whose lives intersected with the great upheavals of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries in unexpected ways. The "Bizarre Organizations" series applies the same approach to institutions, from intelligence agencies to revolutionary cells. And the "Little John" series operates as a kind of adult fairy tale, using the conventions of fantasy narrative to pose questions about human psychology and historical development. Across all these series, he maintains a commitment to what Chinese critics have described as a "people's history" perspective, a historiographical approach that prioritizes the experiences of ordinary individuals over the actions of elites and that seeks to understand historical events through the material conditions and social forces that shaped them.

The linguistic dimension of Xiao Yuehan Kehan's work is arguably as important as its historical content. He has developed a distinctive vocabulary and set of running jokes that his fans refer to collectively as the "Tongliao Universe" (通辽宇宙). The most famous of these is his use of Tongliao itself as a unit of measurement: when describing the area of a foreign country, he will often compare it to his hometown, producing statements such as "Albania is only half a Tongliao." This running gag has become so iconic that "Tongliao" (abbreviated as "T") now functions as a semi-serious unit of area measurement within his community, and the phrase "nT" is used by fans to express the size of any territory. He employs puns, dialect expressions, and colloquial idioms drawn from northeastern Chinese speech, and he has a talent for coining memorable nicknames for historical figures, such as "Soviet Cousin" for Leonid Brezhnev and "American Cousin" for Richard Nixon, that have entered the broader vocabulary of Chinese internet culture. This linguistic creativity has spawned a wave of imitation among other history creators and has been credited with fundamentally altering the style of Chinese online history communication, making it more playful, more accessible, and more attentive to the rhetorical strategies that sustain audience engagement.

The commercial and institutional recognition of Xiao Yuehan Kehan's work has been substantial and consistent. He was named to Bilibili's Top 100 UP Creators list for four consecutive years, from 2021 through 2024, and in 2022 he received the platform's "Highest Popularity" award in addition to his Top 100 designation. In January 2026, he was again recognized as one of the 2025 Top 100 UP Creators. His average video receives over three million views, and his collaboration with Xinhua News Agency in December 2021, a "Hardcore Ruthless People" episode about the British spy George Blake, was widely praised as a model for how independent creators could engage with mainstream institutions without sacrificing their distinctive voice. A commentator at the time observed that the episode demonstrated that "telling China's story does not necessarily require telling a Chinese story," a formulation that captures the universalist ambition underlying his work. In 2023, he co-authored a book titled *Heroes and the Times* with two other history writers, extending his reach from video into print media.

The broader social significance of Xiao Yuehan Kehan's project lies in his demonstration that historical knowledge can be both intellectually rigorous and genuinely popular without compromising either quality. He cites sources and includes reference lists in his videos, yet he presents his material with the pacing and narrative momentum of a serialized drama. His choice of subjects, small nations and obscure individuals rather than great powers and famous leaders, reflects a deliberate political and ethical commitment to expanding his audience's understanding of the world beyond the narrow frame that mainstream media typically provides. For young Chinese viewers, many of whom have limited exposure to the histories of the Global South or to the lived experiences of ordinary people in distant places, his videos offer an education that is both geographically and socially broadening. At the same time, his work has not been without controversy; in 2025, a video in his "Hardcore Ruthless People" series was found to contain serious factual errors, prompting him to issue a public apology and acknowledge that his content production relied on a single external researcher whose sourcing had proven unreliable. His handling of the incident, including a self-deprecating reference to "poor quality control" in a subsequent video, was received by many fans as a genuine acknowledgment of fallibility rather than a defensive deflection, and it arguably strengthened rather than damaged his credibility by demonstrating that he takes his audience's trust seriously.

In summary, Xiao Yuehan Kehan represents a distinctive model of the creator as a public historian, one who treats the video platform as a space for serious intellectual work while refusing to abandon the entertainment value that makes that work accessible to a mass audience. His Tongliao Universe is not merely a collection of running jokes but a coherent rhetorical system that binds together his diverse subject matter and creates a sense of shared community among his viewers. His commitment to a people's history perspective gives his work an ethical orientation that distinguishes it from both conventional academic history and the personality-driven content that dominates much of the platform. And his willingness to acknowledge error and to continue producing work in the face of criticism suggests a maturity that is rare in the often volatile ecosystem of online knowledge production. For Bilibili, he is a cornerstone of the platform's knowledge section and a demonstration that independent creators can achieve both popularity and intellectual seriousness. For viewers around the world, he offers a model of historical storytelling that is rooted in a specific place, Tongliao, but speaks to a universal curiosity about how ordinary people have lived, struggled, and survived in a world shaped by forces far larger than themselves.

entry.title: MediaStorm and Tim Pan: How a Self-Taught Filmmaker Built China's Most Ambitious Video Production Studio on Bilibili
entry.summary: MediaStorm, known in Chinese as Yingshi Jufeng, is a Chinese filmmaking and technology content studio founded and operated by Pan Tianhong, who is universally known by his English name, Tim. Born in 1996 in Hangzhou, Zhejiang Province, Tim is a graduate of the University of…
entry.content:
MediaStorm, known in Chinese as Yingshi Jufeng, is a Chinese filmmaking and technology content studio founded and operated by Pan Tianhong, who is universally known by his English name, Tim. Born in 1996 in Hangzhou, Zhejiang Province, Tim is a graduate of the University of Kent in the United Kingdom, where he studied film. His path to becoming one of Bilibili's most recognized creators was neither linear nor conventional. By his own account and according to media profiles, he was a self-described "internet-addicted teenager" and a poor student during his early years, a young person whose parents and teachers had little reason to expect academic distinction. He left China after middle school to study abroad, eventually earning a degree in film. In 2014, while still a student, he created the MediaStorm account, and in 2015 he uploaded his first video to the internet. After returning to China in 2017, he assembled a small studio team and began producing content focused on filmmaking equipment reviews, technical tutorials, and original short films. What began as a one-person operation has since grown into a company with over 150 employees, annual revenue exceeding one hundred million yuan, and a multi-platform audience exceeding forty million followers, with more than seventeen million on Bilibili alone as of September 2026.

MediaStorm's creative identity is defined by an unusual combination of technical rigor and cinematic ambition. The studio's primary output falls into several overlapping categories: meticulous reviews of cameras, lenses, and production equipment; instructional content that teaches viewers the practical skills of filmmaking, from lighting and composition to editing and color grading; and original short films and documentary projects that demonstrate the techniques being taught. This tripartite structure, in which the studio both explains how filmmaking works and then produces work that exemplifies those principles, distinguishes MediaStorm from creators who specialize in only one mode. The production values of the channel are consistently exceptional; MediaStorm has been described by viewers and critics as "Bilibili's standard-bearer for image quality," a reputation earned through a commitment to shooting in high resolution, employing professional-grade equipment, and investing heavily in post-production. Tim's on-camera presence is similarly distinctive: he is articulate, technically fluent, and visibly enthusiastic about the craft of filmmaking, but he avoids the performative personality-driven style that characterizes many of Bilibili's most popular creators. His videos feel less like entertainment and more like an invitation into a professional workshop, where the viewer is treated as a serious participant rather than a passive spectator.

Among MediaStorm's most significant works is the 2020 documentary "Ascent: We Flew to 30,000 Meters Together," a project that involved launching a high-altitude balloon carrying professional cameras to capture 8K, 360-degree panoramic footage of the Earth's curvature and the near-space environment. The film was not merely a technical demonstration but a narrative about collective aspiration; the team invited viewers to submit photographs and wishes that were attached to the balloon, and the resulting footage was intercut with behind-the-scenes documentation of the preparation and the challenges encountered along the way. The project exemplified MediaStorm's approach to content: ambitious in scope, technically demanding, emotionally resonant, and fundamentally about the process of attempting something difficult rather than the polished result. Other representative works include "We Bought a Chinese Satellite," which documented the studio's collaboration with a domestic satellite manufacturer, and the short film "Little Garlic," which showcased the studio's narrative capabilities beyond technical documentation. The studio's 2023 collaboration with camera manufacturer Insta360 to launch a satellite for Earth imaging represented a further extension of this ambition, blending content creation with genuine technological experimentation.

MediaStorm's platform achievements are substantial and sustained. The channel has been recognized as a Bilibili Top 100 UP Creator for six consecutive years, from 2020 through 2025, and has received the platform's Highest Popularity Award for 2023 and its Diverse Innovation Award for 2022. As of September 2026, the Bilibili channel has 17.42 million followers, and the studio's total footprint across Bilibili, Douyin, Weibo, and Xiaohongshu exceeds forty million followers. The company's commercial performance is equally notable: MediaStorm reported annual revenue exceeding one hundred million yuan in 2024, with profits above ten million yuan, and a single branded T-shirt sold more than two hundred thousand units in a year. Tim was recognized as one of China's "Good Netizens" by the seventh China Youth Good Netizen program in 2024, and in 2025 he was named among Zhejiang Province's top ten "network science communicators". Beyond these formal recognitions, MediaStorm's influence is evident in its capacity to secure collaborations with major technology brands and its participation in high-profile public events, including a 2026 zero-degree snow survival livestream that accumulated 169 million views.

The broader social value of MediaStorm's work lies in its demonstration that technical education and artistic ambition are mutually reinforcing rather than opposed. Tim and his team have built a creative enterprise that treats filmmaking as both a craft to be taught and an art to be practiced, and in doing so they have helped raise the overall standard of video production on Bilibili. Their instructional content has been used by aspiring creators as a practical curriculum, while their original films have shown what is possible when those lessons are applied with sufficient resources and dedication. The studio's willingness to invest in projects with uncertain commercial returns, such as the high-altitude balloon documentary and the satellite collaboration, reflects a commitment to exploration that is rare in a content landscape often driven by algorithmic optimization. At the same time, MediaStorm has not been immune to criticism; observers have noted that the studio's technical strengths do not always translate into nuanced engagement with social or emotional subject matter, and a 2026 incident involving a livestream conflict and subsequent controversy over the studio's workplace culture required a public response from the company. These challenges notwithstanding, MediaStorm's trajectory from a solo YouTube-style channel to a full-fledged production company represents one of the most ambitious and sustained creative projects in the history of Chinese digital media.

In summary, MediaStorm and Tim Pan represent a model of the creator as studio builder, someone who began with a camera and an idea and gradually constructed an institution capable of executing projects that no individual could accomplish alone. Tim's personal story, from a self-described academic failure to the founder of a company with over a hundred employees and a nine-figure revenue, is a narrative about the value of pursuing a genuine passion with discipline and persistence. For Bilibili, MediaStorm is a cornerstone of the platform's aspiration to be a home for serious creative work, not merely entertainment. For aspiring filmmakers and content creators, the studio offers both a practical education and an aspirational vision of what a career in video production can become. And for the broader landscape of Chinese digital culture, MediaStorm is a reminder that the most enduring creative enterprises are those that treat their audience as collaborators in a shared project of exploration and craft.

entry.title: Langhua Jiang: The Storyteller Who Made Chinese History Accessible to Millions
entry.summary: Langhua Jiang, whose real name is Jiang Huajie, is a Chinese history content creator and one of the most distinctive voices in Bilibili's knowledge ecosystem. Born in 1997 in Rizhao, Shandong Province, and currently based in Nanjing, he is a member of the generation that…
entry.content:
Langhua Jiang, whose real name is Jiang Huajie, is a Chinese history content creator and one of the most distinctive voices in Bilibili's knowledge ecosystem. Born in 1997 in Rizhao, Shandong Province, and currently based in Nanjing, he is a member of the generation that Chinese media often refers to as the "post-95s," a cohort that came of age alongside the rise of China's digital platforms. His channel, "Langhua Jiang," which translates roughly to "Waves and Ginger," has accumulated over three million followers across Bilibili and Douyin, with total video views exceeding one hundred million. His self-positioning is deliberately modest: he describes himself not as a historian but as a "storyteller of Chinese history," a phrase that captures both the narrative ambition of his work and his refusal to claim academic authority he does not possess. In less than three years, he has built a body of work that includes series on ancient Chinese daily life, folklore and江湖 culture, and museum artifacts, including a single video lasting four hours and thirteen minutes that surveys all 195 Chinese cultural relics prohibited from overseas exhibition.

Jiang Huajie's path to content creation was neither direct nor instantaneous. Before launching his Bilibili channel in June 2023, he had experimented with WeChat public accounts, podcasts, and vlogs, all without finding a stable audience or a clear creative identity. His breakthrough came with his very first Bilibili upload, a video titled "This Might Be the Best History UP Creator Recommendation on Bilibili," in which he simply recommended other history creators he admired. The video climbed to Bilibili's trending page the following day and quickly surpassed one million views, a result he later described as a "three-way win" in which the recommended creators gained attention, the audience received useful recommendations, and he himself discovered what resonated with viewers. That experience taught him a lesson that would shape his subsequent work: effective communication requires a "利他性," an orientation toward the audience's needs rather than the creator's self-expression. He subsequently produced six or seven more videos before settling on the creative direction that now defines his channel, a gradual process of refinement rather than a single moment of clarity.

What distinguishes Langhua Jiang from the crowded field of Chinese history content creators is his ability to make obscure, often overlooked aspects of the past feel immediately relevant and genuinely fascinating. His videos are organized around several recurring series. The "Chinese Encyclopedia History" series functions as a comprehensive guide to the daily lives of ancient Chinese people, covering topics ranging from clothing and food to the imperial examination system and funeral customs. The "Jianghu History" series explores the folk traditions and underworld stories of bandits, tomb raiders, and con artists that rarely appear in official historical narratives. The "Understanding Museums" series focuses on the artifacts and institutions that preserve China's material heritage. His content is characterized by a relaxed, conversational delivery that avoids academic jargon while still respecting the complexity of his subjects. He has described his approach as "thinning out" history, a metaphor that captures his method of extracting the most engaging and accessible elements from dense historical material without sacrificing accuracy. His videos are long by contemporary standards, often running twenty to thirty minutes, and he has explicitly rejected the pressure to conform to short-video conventions, a decision that has allowed him to build a dedicated audience willing to invest time in substantive content.

Among his most significant works is the 253-minute video "A Complete Tour of China's Top National Treasures in One Episode," released on June 1, 2025. The video surveys all 195 Chinese cultural relics that are prohibited from being taken abroad for exhibition, organized geographically and presented with the same accessible storytelling style that characterizes his shorter content. The production took nearly a year to complete, a period during which he maintained his regular weekly upload schedule simultaneously. The video was selected for Bilibili's "Weekly Must-Watch" list and has accumulated over 2.5 million views, an extraordinary figure for a four-hour history documentary. In an interview, Jiang explained that the project was a long-held personal ambition: he wanted viewers to be able to walk into any museum in China and encounter "familiar faces," artifacts whose stories they already knew. The video's success demonstrates that there is a substantial audience for deep, long-form historical content, even in an era dominated by short-form video. Other notable works include his video "How Did Ancient Chinese People Survive the Coldest Winters?" which accumulated over 2.5 million views within ten days of its release, and his "Chinese Surnames" series, which traces the origins of Chinese family names and has been widely shared among viewers interested in their own ancestral history.

Langhua Jiang's platform achievements reflect the growing prominence of knowledge content on Bilibili. His Bilibili follower count surpassed one million in June 2025, coinciding with the release of his national treasures video, and he has since grown to over three million followers across platforms. His "Chinese Encyclopedia History" series alone has accumulated 120 million views, while other series such as "Chinese Culinary History" and "Jianghu Strange Tales" have each reached tens of millions of views. In 2025, he published a book titled "An Illustrated Guide to Ancient Life and Culture," extending his work from video into print media. He has been recognized with Douyin's Annual Hardcore Content Award, and his videos have been cited in media outlets including The Paper and Southern Metropolis Daily as examples of the "new mass literature and art" movement, a cultural trend in which grassroots creators use digital platforms to make specialized knowledge accessible to general audiences.

The broader social value of Langhua Jiang's work lies in his demonstration that historical knowledge does not need to be simplified or sensationalized to reach a mass audience. He approaches history from the perspective of an ordinary person rather than an academic specialist, and he has argued that this outsider position is precisely what allows him to identify which aspects of the past will resonate with viewers who have no formal training in history. His videos encourage viewers to see history not as a collection of dates and names to be memorized but as a living resource for understanding human behavior, social organization, and cultural continuity. For young Chinese viewers who may feel disconnected from traditional culture, his work offers an accessible entry point that respects their intelligence while meeting them where they are. His emphasis on the "usefulness" of historical knowledge, not in a utilitarian sense but in the sense of enriching one's understanding of the present, aligns with Bilibili's broader mission to position itself as a platform where entertainment and education coexist.

In summary, Langhua Jiang represents a model of the creator as public storyteller, someone who uses digital media to bridge the gap between specialized knowledge and general curiosity. His decision to prioritize long-form, deeply researched content over algorithm-friendly short videos is a calculated risk that has paid off, both commercially and creatively. His background as a self-described "layperson" rather than a trained historian gives his work a relatability that more authoritative voices sometimes lack, while his commitment to accuracy and thorough research ensures that accessibility does not come at the expense of substance. For Bilibili, he is evidence that the platform's knowledge section can support creators who take intellectual risks and expect their audiences to follow. For the broader landscape of Chinese digital culture, he is a reminder that the most enduring content is often that which helps people understand themselves and their world a little better, one story at a time.

entry.title: Mianyang Liaoli: The Culinary Perfectionist Who Turned Recipe Videos into Literature
entry.summary: Mianyang Liaoli, whose real name is Zhang Yi, is a Chinese culinary content creator and one of the most respected figures in Bilibili's food section. A native of Changsha, Hunan Province, she previously worked in program production at Hunan Broadcasting System before founding her own…
entry.content:
Mianyang Liaoli, whose real name is Zhang Yi, is a Chinese culinary content creator and one of the most respected figures in Bilibili's food section. A native of Changsha, Hunan Province, she previously worked in program production at Hunan Broadcasting System before founding her own media company, Changsha Chi Bu Pang Culture Media Co., Ltd. Since uploading her first video, a demonstration of cheese balls inspired by a Hokkaido curry restaurant, on December 22, 2015, she has built one of the most durable careers in Chinese food media, accumulating over 11.9 million followers on Bilibili and more than 86 million total likes as of January 2026.Her channel's name, which translates to "Sheep Cuisine," is a whimsical self-reference, but the work itself is anything but casual. Mianyang Liaoli approaches cooking with the rigor of a researcher and the sensibility of a writer, and in doing so, she has redefined what a food video can be.

Her path into content creation was, by her own account, largely accidental. In a 2022 interview, she explained that she began filming simply to document her kitchen life, and her first upload unexpectedly appeared on Bilibili's homepage, which encouraged her to continue.Her early videos reflected her background in television production: they were slow-paced, gentle, and instructional, closer in spirit to a televised cooking program than to the rapidly edited, personality-driven content that would later dominate the platform. She soon recognized that this style did not suit her temperament. "That overly televised, slow-paced format didn't really match my personality," she recalled, "so I gradually added some popular memes and some absurdist elements."The turning point came when she produced a sponsored video and, worried that the advertisement would feel intrusive, deliberately accelerated the pacing and adopted a style she describes as "deadpan nonsense." The result was a revelation: she had found a voice that was simultaneously irreverent and meticulous, and from that point forward, her videos became exercises in controlled chaos.

What distinguishes Mianyang Liaoli from the crowded field of Chinese food creators is the unusual combination of technical ambition, narrative craft, and linguistic playfulness that defines her work. Her most celebrated videos involve attempts to recreate dishes of extraordinary difficulty: royal recipes from the Qing dynasty, molecular gastronomy showpieces, regional specialties that require days of preparation, and dishes from animated films and video games. The complexity is genuine; she has spent weeks researching and testing a single recipe, and her willingness to document failure alongside success gives her videos an emotional arc that pure instructional content lacks.Her editing style is brisk and densely layered, with quick cuts, sound effects, and visual gags that reward repeat viewing. But her most distinctive signature is her narration. Mianyang Liaoli writes rhyming, rhythmic voice-over scripts that have earned her the official designation of "the rhyming maniac of the culinary world."Her descriptions of food are not merely functional; they are literary. A bowl of clear chicken broth becomes "a mirror-still lake at dawn, unrippled and serene, until a sudden drift of rich, intoxicating savor sends shimmering waves across its glassy surface."Fans have taken to imitating her style in the comments, turning her video sections into impromptu poetry competitions.

Among her most influential works is "Dragon's Chant Strawberry," a recreation of a legendary molecular gastronomy dessert that requires cooking a strawberry through a temperature range spanning from minus 196 degrees Celsius to 99 degrees Celsius.The video became a viral phenomenon, accumulating over 2.35 million likes on Douyin and spawning a wave of imitation attempts across Chinese social media.Her "Sheep's Howl Strawberry," a playful response to her own success, transformed the original concept into a square-shaped confection, demonstrating her ability to build on her own creative output with humor and self-awareness. Other signature videos include her recreation of a Qing imperial recipe that involves stuffing meat into bean sprouts, her attempt to make Indian flatbread and bamboo-pressed noodles at home, and her series of "survival cuisine" tutorials designed for viewers with limited cooking skills and time.Her 2025 original program featuring an AI-designed "interstellar meteorite fried chicken" extended her experimentation into the intersection of artificial intelligence and cooking.The structural variety of her channel, organized around three distinct pillars of elaborate recipe recreation, city food exploration vlogs, and beginner-friendly survival cooking, allows her to serve audiences with vastly different needs while maintaining a coherent creative identity.

Mianyang Liaoli's platform achievements are substantial. She has been selected for Bilibili's Top 100 UP Creators list for six consecutive years, from 2019 through 2024, a distinction that places her among the platform's most consistently recognized creators.Her average video performance is remarkable: her works routinely exceed one million views, with her top videos reaching approximately 16.5 million, 12 million, and 10 million plays respectively.Her fan engagement metrics are equally impressive, with an average of 392,000 likes and 246,000 coin-tips per video, and a follower-to-view ratio approaching sixty percent, indicating that her audience consists largely of dedicated subscribers rather than casual viewers.Beyond Bilibili, she maintains a significant presence on YouTube under the channel name Sheep HoHo, where she has accumulated over 800,000 subscribers, and her total cross-platform following exceeds twenty million.In 2026, she was appointed Chief Content Co-Creation Officer for the 48th World Skills Competition, a role that recognized her ability to communicate the value of craftsmanship to a broad public audience. At the competition's 100-day countdown event, she spoke about her experiences with intangible cultural heritage techniques and traditional snacks, from sugar figurine blowing to bamboo-pressed noodles and Beijing roast duck, observing that only by personally attempting these crafts can one understand the meaning of "one minute on stage, ten years of practice offstage."

The broader social significance of Mianyang Liaoli's work lies in her elevation of cooking from a domestic chore to a subject worthy of intellectual and artistic seriousness. By treating recipes as research projects and food writing as literature, she has helped legitimize culinary content as a form of knowledge production rather than mere entertainment. Her exploration of intangible cultural heritage foods, including her collaborations with traditional craftspeople and her participation in World Skills initiatives, positions her as a bridge between contemporary digital culture and the preservation of artisanal knowledge.For younger viewers who may never attempt her most complex recipes, her videos offer something equally valuable: a model of how to approach any skill with patience, curiosity, and a willingness to fail publicly and try again. Her emphasis on documenting the full process, including the failures and frustrations, rather than presenting only polished results, aligns with Bilibili's broader culture of authentic, process-oriented content and distinguishes her from creators who prioritize visual perfection over genuine instruction.

In summary, Mianyang Liaoli represents a rare synthesis of artistic ambition and audience accessibility. She has built a career on the conviction that cooking is worth taking seriously, not in the sense of solemnity, but in the sense of investing genuine effort, thought, and creativity into every dish. Her rhyming narration, her willingness to spend weeks on a single recipe, and her refusal to condescend to her audience by simplifying the complexity of her subject have earned her a level of loyalty and respect that few food creators achieve. For Bilibili, she is a cornerstone of the platform's food section and a demonstration that knowledge content can be beautiful, funny, and deeply personal. For viewers around the world, she offers a window into Chinese culinary culture that is neither exoticized nor oversimplified, but presented with the care and precision of a craftsperson who believes that the best way to honor a tradition is to attempt it yourself, however imperfectly.

entry.title: GenJi: The Digital Educator Who Built a Million-Strong Classroom on Bilibili
entry.summary: GenJi, whose real name is Li Genji, is a Chinese digital education creator and one of the most prominent figures in Bilibili's knowledge section. Operating under the account name "GenJi Really Wants to Teach You" (GenJi Shi Zhen Xiang Jiao Hui Ni), he has built…
entry.content:
GenJi, whose real name is Li Genji, is a Chinese digital education creator and one of the most prominent figures in Bilibili's knowledge section. Operating under the account name "GenJi Really Wants to Teach You" (GenJi Shi Zhen Xiang Jiao Hui Ni), he has built a following of over ten million users on Bilibili, making him one of the platform's most-followed educational creators. His rise from a university student offering free lectures in borrowed classrooms to a nationally recognized UP creator is a story about the convergence of technical skill, pedagogical conviction, and the expanding reach of China's online knowledge economy. In January 2026, he was named to Bilibili's annual Top 100 UP Creators list, a distinction that confirmed his status not merely as a popular account but as a defining voice in the platform's educational ecosystem.

Li Genji's path into teaching began long before he ever opened a video editing program. As a primary school student, he was already the classmate others turned to for help with difficult problems, a role he describes as his first experience of explaining complex ideas to peers. That instinct followed him into university, where he developed a rare combination of design, programming, and product development skills. He became proficient in front-end and back-end development as well as visual interaction design, and by his early undergraduate years he was already serving as the youngest lecturer at his institution. It was during this period that he identified a disconnect that would shape the rest of his career: many university graduates struggled to find employment not because they lacked intelligence or effort, but because the skills taught in classrooms had little direct application to the demands of the professional world. The gap between what students were learning and what employers actually needed became the problem he set out to solve.

His response was to begin offering free public lectures across universities in central China, covering topics ranging from design tools to programming techniques. The lectures were practical by design, focused on skills that students could immediately apply rather than abstract theory. He continued this practice for nearly a decade, preparing course materials, coordinating venues, and teaching without any financial compensation. The work was demanding and often invisible, but the feedback he received from students who landed jobs or completed difficult graduation projects using what they had learned convinced him that the effort was worthwhile. He founded a student organization called Cloud Workshop (Yunding Zuofang), whose logo, a ladder stretching into the clouds, symbolized his belief that knowledge should function as a ladder for upward mobility. That logo remains on his Bilibili avatar today, a small but telling marker of continuity between his early volunteer teaching and his current platform career.

The transition from offline lectures to online video creation came in 2020, when the pandemic forced him to pause his in-person classes. Rather than abandon the work, he began recording the same practical lessons he had been delivering in person and uploading them to Bilibili. His first upload, a Photoshop tutorial recorded without elaborate production values or scripted performance, accumulated over 1.42 million views. The success was not the result of algorithmic luck but of a simple insight: learners wanted instruction that felt like a real classroom, not a polished entertainment product. GenJi's videos retain that classroom quality. They are structured, patient, and grounded in the assumption that the viewer is genuinely there to learn something useful. His speaking style is direct and unadorned, and his editing favors clarity over spectacle, a deliberate choice that distinguishes him from creators who prioritize production value over instructional substance.

As his audience grew, GenJi expanded his subject matter from design and programming into artificial intelligence, a shift that aligned both with his own technical interests and with the broader cultural moment. His AI-related content explains machine learning concepts, demonstrates practical applications of AI tools, and addresses the anxieties many learners feel about automation and job displacement. He approaches AI not as a distant technological marvel but as a set of tools that ordinary people can learn to use, a framing that has resonated with students, career-changers, and professionals seeking to remain relevant in a rapidly changing economy. His teaching philosophy, which he summarizes as "really wanting to teach you," is embedded in his account name and functions as both a promise to his audience and a standard against which he measures his own work. The phrase captures his rejection of performative education, the kind of content that gestures at learning without delivering it.

The scale of GenJi's platform presence reflects the demand for this kind of instruction. His account has surpassed ten million followers on Bilibili, placing him among the platform's most-subscribed individual creators. He has been featured in Chinese media, including a profile in Youth Daily that traced his evolution from a primary school helper to a digital education pioneer, and his selection for the 2025 Bilibili Top 100 UP Creators list placed him alongside figures like Luo Xiang and Lao Fanqie as one of the platform's defining creators. His influence extends beyond his own channel: he has built a broader educational ecosystem that includes self-developed intelligent hardware and a suite of learning resources designed to make technical skills accessible to users who may not have formal training in computer science. The Cloud Workshop logo on his avatar is a reminder that his project began as a voluntary effort to share knowledge, not as a commercial enterprise, and that the values informing his current work remain rooted in that origin.

The social value of GenJi's work lies in his demonstration that digital platforms can function as genuine educational infrastructure rather than merely as entertainment distribution networks. Bilibili's knowledge section emerged as a significant content category in the late 2010s and early 2020s, and creators like GenJi have been central to its legitimacy. By offering rigorous, practical instruction at no cost to anyone with an internet connection, he has contributed to a broader shift in how Chinese young people think about learning, career preparation, and the relationship between formal education and self-directed study. His emphasis on "knowledge universalization" (zhishi puhui) reflects a conviction that access to practical skills should not be determined by institutional affiliation or economic capacity. For viewers who cannot afford expensive training programs or who live far from major educational centers, his videos offer a pathway to competence that would otherwise be unavailable.

In summary, GenJi represents a model of the creator as educator, someone who treats the platform not as a stage for self-promotion but as a classroom that can accommodate millions of students simultaneously. His decade of unpaid public teaching before his online success is not merely a biographical detail but the foundation of his credibility: he earned his audience by helping people learn, not by chasing trends. His expansion into AI education reflects an awareness that the skills people need are changing, and his willingness to adapt his teaching to new technologies without abandoning his commitment to practical usefulness suggests that his influence will remain relevant as the educational landscape continues to evolve. For Bilibili, he is evidence that the platform's knowledge ambitions are not aspirational rhetoric but measurable reality. For learners, he is a reminder that the most valuable educational content is often the least flashy, and that a teacher who genuinely wants to teach is worth more than a thousand polished performances.

entry.title: Papi Jiang: The First Lady of Chinese Internet Comedy and Her Decade-Long Reinvention
entry.summary: Papi Jiang, born Jiang Yilei on February 17, 1987, in Shanghai, is a Chinese actress, short-video creator, and one of the most enduring figures in the history of Chinese internet culture. She graduated from the Central Academy of Drama with both a bachelor's and a…
entry.content:
Papi Jiang, born Jiang Yilei on February 17, 1987, in Shanghai, is a Chinese actress, short-video creator, and one of the most enduring figures in the history of Chinese internet culture. She graduated from the Central Academy of Drama with both a bachelor's and a master's degree in directing, a background that distinguishes her from the vast majority of Chinese content creators who entered the field without formal training in performance or narrative construction. Her channel on Bilibili, where she is officially certified as a "2018 Top 100 UP Creator" and a "Renowned Comedy UP Creator," has accumulated over 9.4 million followers and more than 1.29 billion total views as of September 2026. But her significance extends far beyond any single platform metric. Papi Jiang is widely credited with legitimizing short-form comedy as a serious creative discipline in China, and her career trajectory, from a graduate student posting videos from her dormitory to a producer overseeing a content studio, offers a case study in how a creator can survive and thrive across multiple cycles of platform evolution.

Papi Jiang's path to internet fame was neither linear nor accidental. She grew up in Shanghai and attended the Shanghai No. 3 Girls' High School, where her saxophone talent in the school's girls' wind band earned her a twenty-point bonus on her high school entrance examination and a guaranteed place in the school's high school division. She was accepted into the Central Academy of Drama's directing program in 2005 and spent her undergraduate years actively involved in theater, both performing in and directing stage productions. After graduation, she explored several professional directions without finding a stable footing, and in 2013, at the age of twenty-six, she made the deliberate decision to return to the Central Academy of Drama for a master's degree in directing. It was during this period of graduate study that she began uploading short comedic videos to Chinese social media platforms, initially as a creative outlet rather than a career strategy. Her breakout came in 2015 and 2016, when a series of videos featuring her signature technique of accelerated voice modulation, rapid costume changes, and sharp observational humor about everyday life went viral across Weibo, WeChat, and Bilibili. By March 2016, she was being described by Chinese media as the "number one internet celebrity of 2016," and her account had attracted millions of followers within a matter of months.

What made Papi Jiang's content distinctive was not merely its humor but its structural sophistication. Unlike the loose, improvisational style that characterized much of Chinese short-form comedy at the time, her videos were tightly scripted, carefully paced, and built around a clear comedic premise that she would explore through multiple character perspectives. In a typical early video, she might play five or six different roles, each representing a recognizable social archetype—the anxious mother, the dismissive boyfriend, the overly competitive colleague—and use rapid cuts and voice changes to create the illusion of a conversation among them. This multi-role technique, combined with her background in directing, gave her videos a theatrical quality that set them apart from the confessional, talking-head format that dominated the platform. Her dialogue was colloquial and often self-deprecating, drawing on the anxieties and absurdities of urban Chinese life: the pressures of marriage and childbearing, the indignities of office politics, the gap between aspirational consumer culture and financial reality. She described herself in her videos with the now-iconic tagline, "I am Papi Jiang, a woman who combines beauty and talent," a line delivered with enough ironic distance to signal that she was fully aware of the absurdity of self-branding in the attention economy.

The commercial and cultural impact of Papi Jiang's early success was unprecedented. In March 2016, she received 12 million yuan in first-round financing from ZhenFund, Logic Show, and two other investment firms, with an estimated valuation of approximately 120 million yuan, making her the first internet celebrity in China to receive venture capital investment. In April of that year, the first commercial placement on one of her videos was auctioned for 22 million yuan, a figure that shocked observers and signaled that short-form video could be a viable advertising medium at scale. This auction is widely regarded as a watershed moment in the professionalization of Chinese content creation, demonstrating that individual creators could command advertising rates comparable to traditional media. In 2018, she was named to Bilibili's inaugural Top 100 UP Creators list, and in the same year, she was appointed Chief Content Officer of Baidu App, a role that placed her at the intersection of content creation and platform strategy. She also co-founded papitube, a multi-channel network focused on incubating and managing short-video creators, which at its peak represented dozens of signed talents and was recognized as one of China's leading MCN organizations.

Papi Jiang's creative output has evolved substantially over the past decade. In the late 2010s and early 2020s, she expanded into acting, appearing in films such as "The Truth About Beauty" and "Wish You Were Here," and taking a supporting role in Wong Kar-wai's acclaimed television series "Blossoms Shanghai," where she played Ling Hong, a boutique owner whose pragmatic, street-smart personality provided a counterpoint to the more romantic protagonists. Her performance was widely praised for its naturalism and comic timing, with critics noting that her background in directing gave her a nuanced understanding of how to build a character within an ensemble. In 2024, she made a significant structural decision: she stepped back from her management role at papitube and returned to full-time content creation, launching a new interview program called "Warm Welcome." The show's format is deliberately minimalist—one table, two chairs, no elaborate sets or scripted segments—and it centers on guests sharing personal recommendations for everyday products while engaging in unguarded conversation. The program became a breakout success, with over 70 million views on Bilibili and 300 million on Douyin, and it was credited with revitalizing the careers of several established entertainers who appeared as guests.

The broader significance of Papi Jiang's career lies in her demonstration that creative longevity on Chinese social media is possible through continuous reinvention rather than mere consistency. She has outlasted the vast majority of her contemporaries from the 2016 "internet celebrity" boom, many of whom faded within a few years. Her ability to move from short-form comedy to acting to interview-based content reflects a willingness to abandon formats that no longer serve her and to invest in new creative challenges even when the commercial incentives favor sticking with proven formulas. For Bilibili, she represents an early bridge between the platform's niche gaming and anime origins and its later emergence as a mainstream cultural force. For aspiring creators, her career demonstrates that a formal education in narrative craft can translate into meaningful advantages in a field that often valorizes spontaneity over discipline. And for the broader landscape of Chinese digital culture, she stands as a reminder that the most durable figures are not those who chase every trend but those who build a body of work that can accommodate growth and change.

In summary, Papi Jiang is not merely a successful content creator but a transitional figure who helped define what Chinese short-form video could be and then repeatedly redefined what her own career could become. Her decade-long presence at the center of Chinese internet culture is a testament to her creative instincts, her willingness to evolve, and her insistence on maintaining a degree of artistic control even as the commercial pressures around her intensified. She remains, in the most literal sense of her own famous tagline, a woman who combines beauty and talent—but more importantly, she combines talent with the discipline and adaptability required to sustain a creative life over the long term.

entry.title: He Tongxue: The Tech Storyteller Who Redefined Digital Creativity on Bilibili
entry.summary: He Tongxue, whose real name is He Shijie, is a Chinese digital technology content creator and one of the most influential figures in Bilibili's technology and knowledge ecosystem. Born in Taiyuan, Shanxi Province, he graduated from the International School of Beijing University of Posts and…
entry.content:
He Tongxue, whose real name is He Shijie, is a Chinese digital technology content creator and one of the most influential figures in Bilibili's technology and knowledge ecosystem. Born in Taiyuan, Shanxi Province, he graduated from the International School of Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications, where he studied telecommunications engineering with a focus on internet of things technology. His channel, "Teacher, My Name Is He Tongxue," which translates roughly to "Teacher, I Am He Tongxue," is a deliberate play on the classroom roll-call convention, signaling from the outset his identity as a student creator speaking to a peer audience. He began uploading videos to Bilibili in October 2017, with his first upload being a simple Premiere tutorial on creating a "door transition" effect. What began as a modest hobby while he was still a university student would, within two years, transform him into a national phenomenon, and within a decade, into a creator with over twelve million followers on Bilibili and a significant international presence through his English-language YouTube channel, HTX Studio.

He Tongxue's entry into content creation was driven less by a desire for fame than by a genuine fascination with how technology works and how it can be explained to ordinary people. His early videos were characterized by a distinctive blend of technical curiosity, cinematic storytelling, and emotional resonance, a combination that set him apart from the conventional tech review format that dominated Bilibili's technology section at the time. Rather than simply listing specifications or benchmarking hardware, he approached each video as a narrative about technology's place in human life, often using himself as the protagonist in a story of experimentation, failure, and eventual discovery. This storytelling instinct, combined with a meticulous attention to visual composition and sound design, gave his work a production quality that rivaled professional media while retaining the intimacy and authenticity of a personal vlog.

The video that launched He Tongxue into mainstream visibility was his June 2019 upload titled "How Fast Is 5G Really?" The video, released just as China was beginning its large-scale rollout of 5G networks, approached the question not through abstract technical explanation but through a series of vivid, relatable experiments.
